```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_ambient <- requireNamespace("ambient", quietly = TRUE)
```

grnland simulates populations whose phenotypes are the steady states of
gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Genotypes are network parameters, development
solves the network dynamics, and selection acts on the resulting phenotypes on
an adaptive landscape of your choice. Because the genotype-phenotype map is a
dynamical system, the variation that mutation produces (the M-matrix) depends
on the network and changes as the population evolves.

The workflow has four steps: define a **model**, map **genotypes to
phenotypes**, define a **landscape**, and **simulate** a population on it.

```{r setup}
library(grnland)
```

## 1. Define a network

Networks are written as edges: `"a -> b"` means *a activates b*, `"a -| b"`
means *a represses b*. Each gene follows Hill-type kinetics,

$$\dot x_i = \alpha_i \prod_j H_{ij}(x_j) - \gamma_i x_i,$$

with production rate $\alpha_i$, decay rate $\gamma_i$, and
$H_{ij}(x) = x^h/(\theta^h + x^h)$ for activation, $1 - x^h/(\theta^h + x^h)$
for repression.

```{r model}
m <- grn(c("a -> b", "b -| c", "c -> a", "a -| c"),
         alpha = c(4, 6, 8), theta = 3,
         evolvable = c("alpha", "theta"),  # parameters that mutate
         traits = c("b", "c"))             # genes under selection
m
```

Any parameter can be a locus: whole classes (`"alpha"`, `"gamma"`, `"theta"`,
`"hill"`) or single entries (`"alpha[b]"`, `"theta[c,a]"`). Genes not listed
in `traits` still develop and regulate, but are invisible to selection.

The six two-gene motifs of the paper are built in:

```{r motifs}
paper_motif(3)   # x1 -> x2, x2 -| x1
```

## 2. Genotype to phenotype

```{r gp}
g <- default_genotype(m)
g
phenotype(m, g)          # steady state of the trait genes
develop(m, g)$status     # 0 = converged to a stable steady state
```

`genotype_at()` goes the other way, finding a genotype that develops into a
target phenotype:

```{r inverse}
mot <- paper_motif(5)
g5 <- genotype_at(mot, c(2, 6))
phenotype(mot, g5)
```

### Sensitivities and the M-matrix

The sensitivity matrix $S = \partial x^*/\partial p$ is computed analytically
from the Jacobian of the dynamics ($S = -J^{-1}\,\partial f/\partial p$). With
per-locus mutation rate $\mu$ and mutational effect $\sigma$, the M-matrix is
$M = S\,\Sigma\,S^\top$ with $\Sigma = \mu\sigma^2 I$ (times the ploidy).

```{r mmatrix}
m_matrix(mot, phenotype = c(2, 6), mu = 0.01, sigma = 0.05)
```

The same phenotype has a differently shaped M under each motif. Here are the
six paper motifs at one phenotype, each scaled to unit trace:

```{r mshapes, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 3}
library(ggplot2)
ellipse <- function(M, n = 100) {
  e <- eigen(M / sum(diag(M)), symmetric = TRUE)
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)
  pts <- cbind(cos(t), sin(t)) %*% diag(sqrt(pmax(e$values, 0))) %*% t(e$vectors)
  data.frame(x = pts[, 1], y = pts[, 2])
}
shapes <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:6, function(k)
  cbind(ellipse(m_matrix(paper_motif(k), phenotype = c(3, 3))), motif = paste("motif", k))))
ggplot(shapes, aes(x, y)) + geom_polygon(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~motif, nrow = 1) + coord_equal() + theme_void()
```

## 3. Landscapes

A landscape is any function from a phenotype matrix (one row per individual)
to fitness values. Constructors cover the common cases:

```{r landscapes, eval = has_ambient}
single <- landscape_gaussian(c(5, 3), omega = 4)              # one Gaussian peak
rugged <- landscape_perlin(frequency = 0.3, seed = 6)         # Perlin noise
twin   <- landscape_smoothmax(landscape_gaussian(c(4, 4), 2),
                              landscape_gaussian(c(7, 7), 2)) # smooth maximum
find_peaks(rugged, lower = 0, upper = 10)
```

`landscape_grid()` caches a slow landscape on a grid and interpolates
bilinearly, which speeds up Perlin landscapes about three-fold in simulations.

## 4. Simulate

```{r sim}
land <- landscape_gaussian(c(5, 3), omega = 4)
sim <- simulate_population(paper_motif(1), land, start = c(2, 6),
                           N = 500, generations = 3000, mu = 0.01, sigma = 0.05,
                           stop = stop_at_peaks(matrix(c(5, 3), 1)),
                           record_every = 20, seed = 1)
sim
head(sim$trajectory)
```

The trajectory records the mean phenotype, the phenotypic covariance matrix
(`P_*`), mean fitness and the number of individuals whose development failed.
Set `record_m = TRUE` to also record the M-matrix at the mean genotype.

Options include:

* `ploidy = 2, reproduction = "sexual"` for diploid sexual populations with
  free recombination (`sexes = TRUE` for separate sexes);
* `selection = selection_proportional()` or `selection_exponential(s)`
  instead of the default of the original scripts (`w - min(w) + 0.001`);
* `invalid = "reject"` to resample offspring whose development fails instead
  of treating them as lethal;
* `stop = stop_at_peaks(peaks)` to stop when the population sits on a peak.

### Different networks, different paths

Even on a single symmetric peak, the network shapes the path. All six motifs
start from the same phenotype and climb the same peak:

```{r paths, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 5}
paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:6, function(k) {
  s <- simulate_population(paper_motif(k), land, start = c(2, 6), N = 500,
                           generations = 3000, record_every = 10, seed = k,
                           stop = stop_at_peaks(matrix(c(5, 3), 1)))
  cbind(s$trajectory[, c("generation", "mean_x1", "mean_x2")], motif = paste("motif", k))
}))
bg <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(0, 7, length.out = 150), x2 = seq(1, 7, length.out = 150))
bg$w <- land(as.matrix(bg))
ggplot(bg, aes(x1, x2)) + geom_raster(aes(fill = w)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey20", high = "grey95", name = "fitness") +
  geom_path(data = paths, aes(mean_x1, mean_x2, colour = motif), linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("point", 2, 6, shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) + labs(x = expression(x[1]), y = expression(x[2]))
```

Motifs whose M has positive covariance between the traits (1, 3, 5) first
move down and to the left, along the long axis of their M, where fitness rises
fastest for the variation they have, and only then turn towards the peak.
Motifs with negative covariance (2, 4) head right, and the unregulated motif 6
takes the most direct route. On rugged landscapes such differences can
decide *which* peak is reached: see the article *Paper figures and examples*.

## Beyond Hill networks

**Custom dynamics.** `grn_custom()` takes any ODE right-hand side, for
regulatory logic the Hill model cannot express (additive inputs, basal
expression). It runs in R and is slower.

```{r custom}
cm <- grn_custom(
  function(x, p) c(p[["a1"]] - x[1],
                   p[["a2"]] * (0.2 + x[1] / (5 + x[1])) - x[2]),
  params = c(a1 = 2, a2 = 2), genes = c("x1", "x2"))
phenotype(cm, default_genotype(cm))
```

**Linear maps.** `gp_linear(B)` gives the linear genotype-phenotype map
$x = B\alpha$, with a constant M-matrix, a useful null model:

```{r linear}
lin <- gp_linear(matrix(c(5, 4, 4, 5) / 3, 2))
m_matrix(lin, phenotype = c(1, 1))
```

**Basins under the Lande equation.** `lande_separatrices()` traces basin
borders for deterministic evolution $\dot{\bar z} = G\,\nabla W$ with
$G \propto M$, which can be compared with simulated outcomes.

**More traits.** Nothing is specific to two traits: networks can have any
number of genes, and `traits` chooses which are selected. Landscapes in more
dimensions can be Gaussian, Perlin (3D) or any function.
